# In Re Relafen Antitrust Litigation
## Headmatter
### Combined Opinion by Young
SmithKline scientist Dr. Carl Rose (“Dr.Rose”) declared that he had obtained solid nabumetone only because he “diverged from [Chatterjea & Prasad’s] described processes in that [he] purified the compounds carefully at each stage.”

The Board of Patent Appeals cited evidence, including Rose’s declaration and SmithKline’s report of obtaining solid na-bumetone “after purification,” which “suggested] that Chatterjea’s ‘thick pale yellow oil’ may well have been an impure form of the claimed compound.”

*Id.* Nor did Judge Lindsay credit the testimony of Drs. Anderson or Rose, who in attempting to distinguish the Chatterjea *&* Prasad publication and SmithKline’s earlier opinions, displayed “visible discomfort” and “easy willingness to recant on cross-examination,” as well as “obstinacy, evasiveness and occasional sophistry.”

Dr. Rose in particular attempted to disclaim earlier statements in a manner that was “generally unconvincing and at times transparently disingenuous.”

Rather, Dr. Rose declared before the Board of Patent Appeals that he had “diverged from the described processes” to obtain solid nabumetone. See Decision of the Board of Patent Appeals at 5 (quoting Rose Deck ¶ 5). On the basis of this and other alleged misrepresentations, the Board of Patent Appeals (mistakenly) concluded that Chatterjea & Prasad’s “thick *367 pale yellow oil” solidified only upon purification.

# United States v. Rose
- **Court** Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
- **Docket number** No. 11-1980
- **Filed**
- **Precedential status** Published
- **Citations** 487 F. App'x 33

OPINION OF THE COURT
RAKOFF, Senior District Judge.
Carl Rose (“Rose”) appeals from his conviction for possessing cocaine and for carrying a firearm in violation of two federal laws. For the reasons set forth below, we affirm.

After a trial that began on January 18, 2011, a jury convicted Rose on three counts: possession of cocaine base with intent to deliver, a violation of 21 U.S.C. § 841(a)(1) & (b)(1)(C); carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1); and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1).

The District Court had jurisdiction over this case under 18 U.S.C. § 3281. Accordingly, we have appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. Rose argues that his conviction must be overturned because the Government relied in its closing argument on evidence that had not been admitted during trial.1

. Rose has also moved to dismiss appellate counsel and proceed *pro se,* arguing that counsel knowingly refused to include certain meritorious issues in the appellate briefs. We construe this as a claim for ineffective assistance of appellate counsel. Such a claim is generally inappropriate on direct appeal. *See United States v. Thornton,* [327 F.3d 268, 271-73](https://courtlistener.com/opinion/781736/united-states-v-michael-benjamin-thornton-michael-thornton/#271) (3d Cir.2003). Accordingly, we will deny Rose’s claim for ineffective assistance of appellate counsel without prejudice to his right to raise this claim on collateral attack.

Petitioner Carl Rose appeals the final decision of the respondent Secretary of Labor denying his request to toll the time for filing his complaint for unlawful termination under the Energy Reorganization Act (“ERA”). For the reasons set forth below, we affirm.

Rose followed this determination with a timely request for a hearing.

For the aforestated reasons, the decision of the Secretary is AFFIRMED.

OPINION OF THE COURT
RAKOFF, Senior District Judge.
Carl Rose (“Rose”) appeals from his conviction for possessing cocaine and for carrying a firearm in violation of two federal laws. For the reasons set forth below, we affirm.

After a trial that began on January 18, 2011, a jury convicted Rose on three counts: possession of cocaine base with intent to deliver, a violation of 21 U.S.C. § 841(a)(1) & (b)(1)(C); carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1); and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1).

The District Court had jurisdiction over this case under 18 U.S.C. § 3281. Accordingly, we have appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. Rose argues that his conviction must be overturned because the Government relied in its closing argument on evidence that had not been admitted during trial.1

. Rose has also moved to dismiss appellate counsel and proceed *pro se,* arguing that counsel knowingly refused to include certain meritorious issues in the appellate briefs. We construe this as a claim for ineffective assistance of appellate counsel. Such a claim is generally inappropriate on direct appeal. *See United States v. Thornton,* [327 F.3d 268, 271-73](https://courtlistener.com/opinion/781736/united-states-v-michael-benjamin-thornton-michael-thornton/#271) (3d Cir.2003). Accordingly, we will deny Rose’s claim for ineffective assistance of appellate counsel without prejudice to his right to raise this claim on collateral attack.
